opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is data, but not simply "we don't have enough data." It's more that we haven't yet found the right form of data and the right objective to scale on.

Look at what made GPT-1 possible. Before it, there was already a huge amount of text on the internet, and people had found a very simple, universal objective: predict the next token. Text is a compressed record of human thinking, so by learning to predict it, the model picks up a lot of structure about the world almost for free. The data existed, the objective was simple, and the two fit together naturally.

In embodied intelligence, we don't have that alignment yet. First, there's no "internet of actions." Robot interaction data is extremely expensive to collect. You need hardware, you need people teleoperating, and every embodiment is different. Data from one robot arm doesn't transfer cleanly to another with different joints, sensors, or grippers. So the data is small, fragmented, and heterogeneous.

Second, we haven't agreed on what the "next token" is for the physical world. Is it the next action? The next frame of video? Some latent state of the world? People are trying all of these: vision-language-action models, world models that predict future video, and so on. Each captures part of the problem, but none has yet shown that clean, predictable scaling behavior where you add more data and compute and the model reliably gets better at things you didn't explicitly train it for. That emergent generalization is really what a GPT-1 moment means to me. It's not about the model being useful yet, it's about seeing the first signal that the recipe works and is worth scaling.

Third, the physical world is unforgiving in a way text is not. With language, a slightly wrong answer is still often acceptable. With a robot, a slightly wrong action means the cup falls. The tolerance for error is much lower, and the feedback loop with the real environment is slow and costly.

So I'd say we're still in the stage of searching for the paradigm. My own view is that video and simulation, essentially learning how the world evolves from large amounts of visual data, may be one of the most promising ways to bridge this gap, because video is the closest thing we have to an internet-scale record of physical interaction. But I don't think anyone can claim we've found the answer yet. When someone finds a data source and an objective that scale together the way text and next-token prediction did, I think that will be the GPT-1 moment for embodied AI.

r001.rationale: The response says robot interaction data is extremely expensive to collect and is small, fragmented, and heterogeneous, explaining why data collection has not scaled effectively.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we haven't yet found the thing that scales. When you look back at GPT-1, what made it a moment wasn't the model itself, which was small and frankly not that impressive. It was that someone had found a recipe: take a simple objective, next-token prediction, feed it a huge pile of data that already existed on the internet, and show that the curve keeps going up as you add more. Everything after that was a matter of money and engineering.

Embodied intelligence doesn't have that recipe yet, and there are three reasons I keep coming back to.

The first is data. Language had the internet, decades of humans writing things down for free. Robotics has nothing comparable. Every trajectory has to be collected by someone teleoperating an arm, or generated in simulation and then you fight the sim-to-real gap, or scraped from human video where you have to guess at the actions. None of those scale the way text scaled. People are collecting data, and the datasets are getting bigger, but we're talking about something closer to tens of thousands of hours, not trillions of tokens.

The second is that we don't agree on the objective. Next-token prediction was almost embarrassingly simple, and that simplicity is why it worked across every domain. In embodiment, what's the equivalent? Predict the next action? Predict the next frame? Predict the next world state? Each lab has a different answer, and they lead to different architectures and different data requirements. Until one of those wins convincingly, you can't get the whole field pushing on the same curve.

The third one is more subtle. Language models could be useless for a long time and still get funded, because evaluating them was cheap. You could look at the samples and feel the progress. With a robot, the evaluation is physical. It takes hours, it breaks things, and a policy that's 80 percent right is often worse than nothing because the 20 percent is a dropped glass. So the feedback loop between research and the next experiment is slow, and that slows the whole field down.

What I'd say is that we're probably in the pre-GPT-1 phase in a good sense. The ingredients are visible. Vision-language models give us a prior for understanding scenes. World models are getting good enough that you can imagine them as a data engine. And the hardware is finally cheap enough that many groups can run the same experiments. My guess is the moment comes when someone shows that a single, boring objective trained on a mix of real and generated data keeps improving as you add more of both. The first version of that will look unimpressive, just like GPT-1 did. But it'll be the thing everyone copies.

r001.rationale: The response says robotics lacks a scalable data source and explains that trajectories must be collected through teleoperation, simulation, or inferred from video, none of which scale like internet text.

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason is that we haven’t yet found a scalable learning recipe for embodied intelligence. In language, you have a relatively unified interface—text—and a huge amount of data in that format. In robotics, the data is fragmented across different bodies, sensors, environments, and tasks. An experience collected by one robot isn’t automatically useful to another.

And the data is much harder to collect. A robot has to interact with the world, and that takes time. When it fails, you may need a person to reset the environment. Video can help a model learn what the world looks like, but it doesn’t directly tell it what action to take, how much force to apply, or how to recover when something goes wrong.

So, to me, a GPT-1 moment wouldn’t just be an impressive robot demonstration. It would be evidence that a general training approach transfers across tasks, and that adding more data and compute reliably improves that transfer. We have promising pieces, but we haven’t yet established that scaling loop.

r001.rationale: The candidate says embodied intelligence lacks a scalable learning recipe, then explains that robot data is fragmented and costly to collect through real-world interaction. This communicates the lack of an effective way to scale data collection.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason is that we haven’t yet found a scalable way to connect data, a learning objective, and a general-purpose model for embodied intelligence.

For language, you can collect a huge amount of text and train a model to predict the next token. That gives you a fairly consistent learning signal across many different tasks. In robotics, the data is much more fragmented. Different robots have different bodies, sensors, and action spaces. Even the same action can produce different results depending on the environment. So collecting more data doesn’t automatically mean you can train a more general model.

There’s also a difference in the cost of interaction. A language model can learn from text that already exists. A robot often needs to act in the world to gather useful experience, and that takes time. Simulation can help, but then you have to make sure what it learns transfers to the physical world.

So, to me, the question is whether we can establish a learning framework where more diverse experience reliably leads to better capabilities across tasks and embodiments. We have promising pieces, but I don’t think that loop is established yet. When it is, we may look back and call that our GPT-1 moment.

r001.rationale: The response says the main reason is the absence of a scalable way to connect data, a learning objective, and a general-purpose model, and explains that embodied data is fragmented and costly to gather.
